title: Compose `dns` field has no effect on the created container
body:
### Issue Description

I've spent the last week trying to get pi-hole running properly, and right now I've found that the only way for the `dns` option in my `compose.yml` file to have any impact on the container's `resolv.conf` file is to set it to `none`, so that it doesn't generate at all. This, of course, fixes the issue of not having DNS working for that container, but, unless I've misread anything (likely), it would leave the container without Aardvark.  

Now, the reason I'm trying to do this is that DNS seems to just be broken within the container:
```
$ nslookup example.com
;; communications error to 10.89.0.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 10.89.0.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 10.89.0.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to fdcd:258d:ba75:f804::1#53: timed out
;; no servers could be reached
```



### Steps to reproduce the issue

Steps to reproduce:

1. Create the following `compose.yml`:
```
services:
  test:
    container_name: test
    image: busybox:latest
    command: "tail -f /dev/null"
    dns: 1.1.1.1
```
2. Run `sudo podman compose up -d`
3. Run `sudo podman exec test cat /etc/resolv.conf`.
4. **DNS 1.1.1.1 is nowhere to be seen.**
5. Run `sudo podman exec test nslookup example.com`
6. **Nslookup fails: `;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached`**

### Describe the results you received

Compose ignored the DNS field and as a result the container has no working DNS provider.

### Describe the results you expected

DNS should be working one way or another, either by adding an entry to `resolv.conf` or forwarding queries to `1.1.1.1` somehow.

comments.body:
The nameserver is not written in resolv.conf because that is the aardvark-dns ip which must be used to allow inter network name resolution. Arrdvark-dns itself will receive the nameserver ip for the container and knows how to forward accordingly.

From your output the issue is not that the field is not used, the problem is aardvark-dns is not reached at all. Given you use sudo I assume you run rootful podman. That means aardvark-dns will try to bind port 53 on the host on the network interface.
So make sure that while the container is running that the aardvark-dns process is running and listing on the port. If it is running check you firewall rules on the host, most likely your ruleset blocks incoming connecting to port 53 from the container.

And as general thing we do not support compose directly, so it would be good to rule out any problems there by using proper podman commands.
```
podman network create test
podman run --network test --name test busybox:latest nslookup example.com 
```

Hey there! Sorry for the late reply. I tried out all of your suggestions, and I have a question, as well:
What do you mean exactly by 'compose isn't supported directly'? It may be a good time to mention I'm pretty new to podman. Is there an alternative to compose I should be using instead? If so, and if it's no bother to you, could direct me somewhere I can learn more about it? I'd really appreciate it.

### Compose
I ran the podman commands you provided and can confirm it's not just because I'm using compose:
```
$ sudo podman network create test
test
$ sudo podman run --network test --name test busybox:latest nslookup example.com
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
```

I also got the idea of inspecting both the pihole container and network to see if the `dns` key had any impact, and it indeed shows up here (heavily redacted for brevity, of course):
```
$ sudo podman inspect pihole
...
               "CreateCommand": [
                    ...
                    "--dns",
                    "1.1.1.1",
                    ...
               ]
...
```
I also ran `network inspect` just to be thorough, but there was no sign of `1.1.1.1` being set as the DNS server, which tracks, given that the key is per-service and not per-network.

### Aardvark
> That means aardvark-dns will try to bind port 53 on the host on the network interface.

Assuming by network interface you mean podman's, then yes, aardvark successfully binds to port 53 while the container is running:
```
$ sudo ss -tlnp | grep 53
LISTEN 0      128                   10.89.0.1:53         0.0.0.0:*    users:(("aardvark-dns",pid=9177,fd=12))
LISTEN 0      128    [fdcd:258d:ba75:f804::1]:53            [::]:*    users:(("aardvark-dns",pid=9177,fd=14))
```

### Firewall
I've had a lot of hiccups since I manage my firewall with UFW (yeah, I know). I thought of this and created an explicit 'allow forward' rule for the podman subnets (maybe it's not enough?):
```
$ sudo ufw status verbose
Status: active
Logging: on (low)
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), deny (routed)
New profiles: skip

# I redacted the rest of the allow rules for security and brevity, of course:
To                         Action      From
--                         ------      ----
10.89.0.0/24 DNS           ALLOW FWD   Anywhere                  
Anywhere                   ALLOW FWD   10.89.0.0/24
Anywhere (v6)              ALLOW FWD   fdcd:258d:ba75:f804::/64  
```
Please note:
- There are no non-route rules for the podman interface as I would expect all outgoing traffic to go through the other two interfaces, and the default policy for outgoing traffic is `allow`.
- I'm allowing all traffic to be forwarded from any podman interfaces indiscriminately (not proud of this, I'd like to constrict it but first I need to get it working of course)

### Experiments (edit): 

I'll be running some more experiments while I wait for your response and will edit this comments if I find anything noteworthy.

Okay, this thing took me an embarrassing amount of time to pull off, but here's the gist: I still have no idea why UFW is blocking outgoing DNS requests for my pihole container, BUT, here's what I did, maybe you can spot something I couldn't:

1. On the host machine, I ran this squeaky thing: `sudo watch -n 1 "sudo journalctl -kr | grep -i -E 'block.*(src=10|src=fdcd).*PT=53'"`. It shows only dropped packets sent by any podman address that involve port 53.
2. I ran `sudo podman run -it --rm --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_ADMIN docker.io/instrumentisto/nmap:latest 1.1.1.1 -v -p 53` on the host machine (I also tested it without the added capabilities, just need to include the arguments `-sT` and `-Pn`)
3. When it, of course, failed, I could see that the subnet address used by these standalone tests was `10.88.0.0/24` instead of `10.89.0.0/24`, so I
4. Ran `sudo ufw route allow from 10.88.0.0/24`.
5. Now, I redid step 2, and voilá! It's now working:
```
PORT   STATE SERVICE
53/tcp open  domain
```
6. I then noticed that the same rule (only using `10.89.0.0/24` instead) doesn't have the same effect on the pihole container:
```
# The pihole container does not count with the nmap utility
$ sudo podman exec pihole nslookup example.com
;; communications error to 10.89.0.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 10.89.0.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 10.89.0.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to fdcd:258d:ba75:f804::1#53: timed out
;; no servers could be reached
```
7. And the monitoring tab (see step 1) showed the following dropped packets:
```
sep 29 21:54:07 kernel: [UFW BLOCK] IN=podman1 OUT= MAC=9a:cb:0a:68:ba:99:be:d4:0c:65:40:70:86:dd SRC=fdcd:258d:ba75:f804:0000:0000:0000:0002 DST=fdcd:258d:ba75:f804:0000:0000:0000:0001 LEN=77 TC=0 HOPLIMIT=64 FLOWLBL=794635 PROTO=UDP SPT=40085 DPT=53 LEN=37
sep 29 21:54:02 kernel: [UFW BLOCK] IN=podman1 OUT= MAC=9a:cb:0a:68:ba:99:be:d4:0c:65:40:70:08:00 SRC=10.89.0.2 DST=10.89.0.1 LEN=57 TOS=0x00 PREC=0x00 TTL=64 ID=5539 PROTO=UDP SPT=57521 DPT=53 LEN=37
sep 29 21:53:57 kernel: [UFW BLOCK] IN=podman1 OUT= MAC=9a:cb:0a:68:ba:99:be:d4:0c:65:40:70:08:00 SRC=10.89.0.2 DST=10.89.0.1 LEN=57 TOS=0x00 PREC=0x00 TTL=64 ID=54926 PROTO=UDP SPT=34417 DPT=53 LEN=37
sep 29 21:53:52 kernel: [UFW BLOCK] IN=podman1 OUT= MAC=9a:cb:0a:68:ba:99:be:d4:0c:65:40:70:08:00 SRC=10.89.0.2 DST=10.89.0.1 LEN=57 TOS=0x00 PREC=0x00 TTL=64 ID=25148 PROTO=UDP SPT=34636 DPT=53 LEN=37
```
In my eyes, there's no apparent reason why the firewall would be dropping these packets for this specific environment. There must be something else besides the `route allow` rules.

### Finally
Thanks for taking the time to help me out! And for not using AI for actually writing your responses. That actually means a lot to me. I know this turned out to be quite a lot of text, and not all of it may be relevant, so I went out of my way to make it a little nicer on the eyes. I sincerely hope it helps.
